When designing modern web applications and microservices using the Spring ecosystem, understanding the exact tier-based semantics of @Controller, @RestController, and @RequestMapping is vital for routing HTTP traffic, managing serialization boundaries, and handling view rendering. At the root of this hierarchy is @RequestMapping, the core meta-annotation responsible for mapping web requests onto specific handler methods and classes. Whether operating inside a traditional Spring MVC servlet container or a reactive Netty-backed WebFlux application, @RequestMapping abstracts URL path matching, HTTP methods, and media type constraints.

Building upon this foundation, @Controller is a specialized stereotype annotation that tells the Spring IoC container to treat the annotated class as a web controller, typically returning HTML views via engines like Thymeleaf or FreeMarker. However, with the rise of single-page applications and JSON/XML-based microservices, Spring introduced @RestController as a specialized convenience composite. Combining @Controller and @ResponseBody, @RestController automatically serializes return values directly into the HTTP response body using registered HttpMessageConverters, eliminating the need to manually annotate every single method with @ResponseBody.

items: The @RequestMapping annotation can be applied at both the class and method levels. Class-level mapping acts as a shared URI prefix or namespace, while method-level mapping refines the path, query parameters, headers, and HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH).

@RestController is a textbook example of a composed annotation. Under the hood, Spring processes the presence of @ResponseBody on the meta-annotation during bean post-processing, configuring the handler adapter to bypass view resolution altogether.

In Spring WebFlux, these annotations map seamlessly onto reactive return types such as Mono and Flux, where the underlying framework leverages non-blocking codecs (like Jackson 2 JSON encoder over Netty ByteBuffers) to stream data back to the client as chunks become available.

parsed_answer.content: A common production gotcha occurs when developers mix up @Controller and @RestController inside an API project. If you use a plain @Controller and forget to append @ResponseBody on a method meant to return JSON data, Spring's DispatcherServlet will interpret the returned object's string representation as a physical view name (e.g., trying to resolve a view named 'UserDto(id=1, name=John)' to a file like '/WEB-INF/jsp/UserDto(id=1, name=John).jsp'), resulting in a frustrating Whitelabel Error Page or a 404 Not Found.
